items.summary: Paper P10 of a ten part series P1-P10 on Interaction, Cohesive Emergence, and Fundamental Constants in Generalised Trace Dynamics P10 — Synthesis, physical compatibility and fundamental constants Can the exceptional algebras that organise candidate particle properties also describe the dynamics that selects them? We give a pedagogical research synthesis of nine studies of interacting generalised trace dynamics and its finite matrix extensions. Interactions between spacetime--matter atoms are motivated by bosonic exchange between fermionic currents. An ordered coassociative vertex, its graded selection rules and a positive mediated kernel make this proposal calculable. A selected physical-current model has a common onset of two neutral composite condensates, while separate matrix parents exhibit exact ordering bounds, competing geometric configurations and finite-time record protocols. A trace isometry connects a spin-one matrix sector to exceptional Jordan invariants. For one exact canonical fermion determinant, a positive-squares identity proves that commuting equilateral configurations, rather than the Jordan-bearing balanced branch, are selected sufficiently close to onset. A complementary exact result shows that the polynomial parent's cubic selects associative orientations of the balanced spin-one branch, whose centred Jordan spectrum is a degenerate doublet. Equal spacing is not stationary under those unrestricted orientation variations. Massive canonical fermions can provide positive local orientation curvature, but cancellation of the cubic slope and full vacuum stability are separate conditions. A further fixed-charge parent supports a stable local branch whose Jordan response requires additional collective coordinates. Conserved charges then produce a calculable, coordinate-invariant difference between relaxed static and closed-system slow spectral response. These results put earlier mass-ratio, mixing and gauge-normalisation proposals into contact with explicit vacuum and response calculations. They also identify their remaining inputs: the microscopic physical projection, state, relative family frames, kinetic residues and matching data. Full cohesive emergence of spacetime, matter and classical records, and the measured fundamental constants, have not been derived. The interaction is required to preserve the additive STM sector's conditional spectral framework. Recovery at zero coupling does not establish this compatibility at finite coupling; we formulate the missing projection and backreaction tests explicitly. The achievement is a set of constructive bridges and discriminating tests, with a concrete route from algebraic hypotheses to physical predictions.

items.summary: Tomographic reconstruction is challenging because of limited angular coverage, noise, specimen motion and radiation damage. Here, I present GRECO, Geometric Registration of Electron Cryotomography Observations, an algorithm that uses local specimen structure to fit a shared three-dimensional geometry. Starting from central views, it selects landmarks from a working reconstruction and progressively adds neighbouring views. Near zero tilt, uncertainty in landmark depth has less effect on the predicted image position, allowing provisional landmarks to guide the first steps. Each landmark contributes through views with useful local information. For each observation, GRECO reconstructs a local reference from the other supporting views and compensates for the directional blur produced by those viewing angles. A joint fit updates image translations and landmark positions, linking overlapping angular tracks across the series. GRECO produced reconstructions suitable for subtomogram averaging, detection of small macromolecular complexes and detailed membrane segmentation across specimens ranging from vesicles with fiducials and a fiducial-free mixture to an intact near-minimal cell and cellular lamellae imaged in situ. The Greco software combines this registration algorithm with fast preprocessing, reconstruction and TinyCARE denoising, providing a practical workflow for studying molecular structure and cellular organization.

items.summary: Complete derivative bounds can be too large for a continuation estimate even when the contractions actually used in that estimate occupy restricted tensor slots. We prove that every eligible third derivative in the constrained response budget of a fixed Lorentzian simplicial source has two independently varied normal arguments. An admitted normal–normal–full bound therefore replaces the unrestricted third-derivative coefficient in those terms. The proof retains the full complex normal covector, both inverse denominators, the actual-graph Schur cost, and the separate unrestricted second and fourth derivatives. A noncircular argument uses an already established regular source product to admit the graph and homotopies, and checks the fourth-derivative shoulder separately in the original action domain. For each of two identified branches, fresh complete source records and exact rational assembly verify a locally unique real stationary section on [1536,24576]τ, where τ = 2−61, in normalized balls of radius 2−32 about the exact tangent predictor at 3072τ. The common predictor-error bound is 3.25241355 10−13. Actual-root overlaps and the supplied post-publication bridge connect the stationary range to [3,24576]τ. Holding the geometry, source records, tangent enclosures, mixed inverse and value-response bound fixed, the typed calculation passes all four declared tests; the unrestricted-response comparison fails the residual and required-error budgets. Its larger sufficient residual ceiling differs by approximately 288.32 on the worst branch. The conclusion remains conditional on the explicit source, analytic membership and directed-enclosure premises. This manuscript records executed numerical evidence and an assessed paper-specific Lean supporting subset. The latter establishes conditional finite-dimensional, scalar, geometric, exact-arithmetic, overlap and recovery results; it does not formalize the physical action or the complete analytic existence and source-membership argument.

items.summary: Abstract: Classical inferential statistics and p-value hypothesis testing in healthcare big data repositories suffer from severe structural limitations, notably p-hacking, asymptotic N-bias, and the frequent violation of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumptions due to intra-patient longitudinal dependencies, hospital clustering, and epidemiological shockwaves. To overcome these failures, we introduce an Inverse Breakpoint Analysis, a scale-invariant, physics-inspired metrological audit framework. Our analysis treats discrete clinical event counts not as abstract probabilities, but as physical informational mass. Grounded in Garwood exact discrete limits and Wilson-Hilferty approximations, the framework extends our previous work on stress testing indices for Big health data and establishes three rigorous thresholds: a pure mass saturation limit, a baseline tolerance band, and a structural signal threshold. Through the use of these three parameters, our inverse break-point analysis eliminates false-positive artifacts induced by massive repository sizes while preventing under-powering in small cohorts. Ultimately, the framework demonstrates that percentage-based thresholds are kinematic artifacts of scale, whereas absolute excess discrete mass serves as the sole physical invariant for healthcare data validation. We validated this approach with numerous illustrative examples.
items.title: Inverse Breakpoint Analysis: A Scale-Invariant Physics-Inspired Metrological Audit for Sanitary Big Data

items.summary: This Version 2.1 report places the Maxwell Mass Effect at the forefront of a coherent model for the Venusian atmosphere. The surface temperature is treated as the dependent variable required to support the atmospheric mass against gravity. Solar energy is captured in a shallow topside thermal heating pool, stored as potential energy, and returned to depth by organised descent in the polar vortices under conservation of angular momentum. The sulfuric-acid lifting condensation level (LCL) acts as the thermodynamic anchor (Dew-Point Anchor Hypothesis). A two-component radiative opacity lapse rate then fixes only the geometric separation between that LCL and the infrared emission level. Stochastic inverse modelling with a VIRA equatorial profile, hydrostatic integration and thermodynamic filters recovers a cloud base near 49.6 km, an emission level near 69.4 km at approximately 229 K, and a surface pressure of approximately 91.5 bar. An order-of-magnitude energy-budget test shows that the required polar mass flux lies within the range of observed vortex descent speeds. Version 2 adds a quantitative recirculation (recycle) test using existing Venusian meridional circulation wind data. Observed poleward flows of ~10–15 m s⁻¹ at cloud tops imply a hemispheric Hadley-cell mass flux of order 10¹¹ kg s⁻¹ and a full recirculation timescale of 1–2 weeks. This multi-cycle pathway resolves the apparent single-pass temperature-rise tension and brings the adiabatic signature into agreement with observed polar temperature contrasts of 15–50 K. The same boundary conditions can be satisfied by a conventional greenhouse calculation, but only the Maxwell framework supplies a structural explanation for the polar vortices themselves and a dynamically consistent energy pathway. A new Discussion section explains the changes from Version 1 and how they address independent criticisms of the energy-budget magnitude and the need for a discriminating quantitative test. Diagnostic figures from the inverse model and the recirculation test are included.
items.title: The Maxwell Mass Effect as a Model for the Venusian Atmosphere

items.summary: When a security commitment is defended by an organised interest, the interest may have preceded the commitment, grown out of it, or been built on purpose by its sponsor. These three readings come from interest-group research, policy-feedback research and research on designing policies to last, and are rarely set side by side. We make them testable and apply them to attempts to end security commitments in the United States and Europe after 1945. The dependent variable is the survival of a commitment under an attempt to reverse it, not the level of spending. In the United States cases (the B-1 bomber, the F-22 and C-17, the F136 alternate engine, the closure of military bases, and all programmes proposed for termination in 2009), the breadth of a programme's supplier spread does not decide its survival: the F-22 and the C-17, with suppliers in 44 and 43 states, had opposite fates in 2009. Three findings follow. The legislature's own record can be the defending interest: programmes Congress had created or restored against the executive survived where programmes it had merely funded did not. Executive pressure can be graded from the Statements of Administration Policy: the only unconditional veto threat ended its programme, while conditional threats and objections did not end programmes Congress owned. And what protects a commitment is whether its central defenders can be compensated, down to the production site. In Europe, as the European Defence Fund's rules are rewritten, the veto member states wrote for themselves is extended while the Commission's rule for spreading benefits is made optional. We register one prediction on the Fund's successor. The evidence extends to material published on 1 November 2026, including reporting on member-state divisions over the European Competitiveness Fund.
items.title: Grown or Built? Interests that Defend Commitments after 1945

items.summary: Resolution Geometry: A Kernel–Stabilizer Geometry of Observability Abstract Resolution Geometry (RG) is a protocol-explicit framework for characterizing what a declared observation system can distinguish, preserve, and consistently infer. Its starting point is a family of observation laws together with admissible outcome relabelings, rather than a covariance decomposition, metric, or dynamical model. Equality of the joint observation law defines a kernel groupoid and an observational quotient, canonically identified with the law image. An experiment-internal quantity is identifiable precisely when it is constant on observational fibres. The quotient alone determines neither a metric nor a connection, causal structure, clock, physical scale, or law of motion. The framework separates exact observational equivalence from statistical distinguishability, admissibility, symmetry, and physical realization. The stabilizer of the observation law induces a faithful effective action on the quotient. Liftable symmetry is distinguished from symmetry of the law image: the former can depend on the latent presentation, whereas the observable layer is presentation-invariant once its law-space structures and declarations are fixed. On regular strata, natural modules defined by pullback from law space descend uniquely to the observational quotient. This gives representative independence and projectability for law-defined structures, without asserting that naturality selects those structures. In regular classical experiments, the Fisher tensor supplies infinitesimal distinguishability under the stated Markov-monotonicity assumptions; its radical agrees with the observational vertical space under the corresponding regularity conditions. Quantum protocols require a declared operational task to select within the family of monotone metrics. A central organizing result concerns task-preserving conversion . For a representation map and a declared family of downstream tasks, RG characterizes the exact set of compatible task outcomes on each representation fibre. Unique inference is possible exactly when this residual is a singleton. Otherwise the appropriate output is a correspondence or a typed abstention, not an arbitrary hidden representative. Pairing a representation with its tasks gives a terminal sufficient refinement. For declared operations, observational closure is expressed by the greatest operation-stable congruence contained in the observation kernel. These constructions distinguish local differential rank, global orbit separation, observational completeness, and reconstruction, and make preservation requirements explicit under composition. Second-order realizations provide concrete classification and computational tools. Under a declared block-orthogonal gauge, a covariance datum is encoded by a symmetric matrix tuple whose ordered word traces form a complete pointwise invariant, including repeated eigenvalues, vanishing couplings, and rank-deficient sectors. On simple-spectrum strata, mixed moments recover coupling magnitudes, while independent cycle holonomies complete the residual sign classification. This distinguishes hidden values omitted by a descriptor from distinctions that are genuinely observationally null . Under the different contract of covariance-preserving block-linear transformations, canonical correlations with multiplicity classify pointwise data; constant-type families additionally carry bundle and gluing information. Pointwise classification therefore does not replace the transport, relative alignment, or global data required by field-level tasks. Across rank, symmetry, and protocol changes, RG uses specialization maps when kernel inclusion permits them and correspondences otherwise. Smooth geometry is confined to its regular domain; proper-groupoid and tame settings support stratified descriptions with slices, tangent cones, and orbit-type changes. Finite-resolution statements are separated from exact model state

items.summary: Everything needed to redo the two analyses reported in the Technical Note named in the title, and nothing else. What is here the secondary analysis of published length-resolved binding: the contract frozen before any test statistic was computed and its two dated amendments, the resampling of the source's own trimmed-mean procedure, the anchored and anchor-free tests, the post-hoc robustness check across five normalisation variants, the superseded first run kept so the correction stays visible, and the figure generator; the two propositions behind the simulation and the script that checks both against the stored benchmark, per replicate; the simulated measurement study it checks: frozen primary and stress designs, the finite-chain engine, 7,200 simulated datasets under seven observation operators reported as all 302,400 planned rows including the undefined, outside-window and non-identified slots, an independent validator, the stress results, five focused tests, an 83-file manifest and a dependency lock; an 80-value subset of the Source Data for Fig. 2B/C of Sheikh et al., Nat. Commun. 13, 3617 (2022), with its sheet coordinates. These values keep the original article's CC BY 4.0 licence and attribution; the rest of the archive is under the MIT licence in LICENSE. Reproducing The added analysis runs from the archive root with the standard library plus NumPy; the README gives the four commands. It was re-run on an interpreter far older than the one that produced the shipped results (Python 3.7.6 with NumPy 1.19.1, against 3.13.17 with 2.5.3): the proposition checks were identical in all 520 compared values apart from the recorded environment, and three bootstrap interval endpoints differed in their last digits, by at most 1.5e-11. Figures redraw with the same layout; their byte sequences depend on which sans-serif face the host has. The base study's own replay script requires bit equality and returns a failure on Linux, where ten of its twenty tables differ in their last digits. What is deliberately not here the manuscript text; the original publisher workbook of Sheikh et al. and every panel of it other than the 80 values used; historical MCMC traces and the exploratory transcript analysis of an earlier, separate study, which this work does not use; correspondence and author-only files. REDACTION.md lists the three files whose description of the work was restated for publication, with the digest before and after; no number, method, decision rule or result changed. Scope Synthetic counts are idealised events, not biological replicates. The site-equivalent pool is not an alpha-dystroglycan molecule count, glycan mass, antibody intensity or muscle force. The published array values are technical replicates of one experiment, and the source states no independent experiments. No real assay's detection ceiling or recovery function is measured anywhere in this archive.

items.summary: This repository provides three physics-based datasets for developing and evaluating surrogate models to identify the seismic failure modes (SFMs) of coastal reinforced concrete bridge bents supported by pile-group foundations under combined scour and corrosion. Each sample contains 20 input variables: 17 structural and geotechnical parameters, scour depth, and the corrosion levels of longitudinal and transverse column reinforcement. The output is one of three SFMs: column flexural failure (CFF), foundation flexural failure (FFF), or column shear-associated failure (CSF). These labels are determined through nonlinear finite element analysis and code-based shear capacity calculations. The datasets support reproducible surrogate model development and subsequent life-cycle probabilistic assessment of SFMs and their transitions in deteriorating coastal bridge bents.
items.title: Seismic Failure Mode Datasets for Coastal Pile-Group-Supported Bridge Bents Subjected to Scour and Corrosion

items.summary: Surface code decoders like Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) can also be used to estimate or bound the probability of a logical failure conditioned on the error syndrome commonly called ``soft outputs''. Estimates like the complementary gap of a matching, or others like the ``cluster gap'' are used to produce high fidelity magic states via post-selection. They are also helpful in reducing the overhead of fault-tolerant computation via code concatenation schemes like yoked surface codes. In this work we provide techniques to tightly lower bound the complementary gap of a rotated surface code syndrome block and provide fast parallel algorithms for computing this lower bound efficiently. Our algorithms run in real time for the moderate distances and reasonable physical noise rates required by these applications. We achieve latencies of the order of one to tens of microseconds on sufficiently fast CPU cores.
items.title: Fast Bounds on Matching Decoder Soft Output for the Surface Code

items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents embedded in software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms inherit the user's permissions. When a permission is revoked during a task, the platform rejects the next read, but the agent still retains the data it previously retrieved in its context, drafts, saved documents, and memory. This study examined how platforms can enforce a mid-task revocation on that working state. The author defined correct behavior for four revocation types, each mapped to an obligation to block, purge, or suspend, including leaks through paraphrases, aggregates, and existence hints. The author built RevBench, a simulated field-service platform, and compared nine enforcement designs from access control, information-flow control, and machine unlearning on six frontier models in 6,048 runs. Outputs were scored using exact matching and two large-language-model judges. Per-call authorization still failed in 417 of 720 runs (57.9%), rising from 34.4% when the revocation preceded retrieval to 72.8% when it followed delivery. Information-flow labels leaked the least (12.9%) but left revoked data saved in 44.2% of runs. Designs that invalidated the context performed best, while editing the context in place left derived facts behind. A full restart and selective replay with listing-level provenance reached 21.4% and 21.0% substantive failure, the latter with 12.1% fewer model calls. Most remaining failures were disclosures about the restriction, often repeating the platform’s own notice, and larger models did not reduce them. SaaS platforms need revocation controls that reach the agent’s working state and match the type of revocation. items.summary: Phase-fixed weighted Gerchberg-Saxton (WGS) is the practical method for large arrays of optical traps, but it optimizes the hologram on an ideal model of the spatial light modulator (SLM), and the sequences that move traps interpolate between holograms that were never optimized for the frames in between. We test two hypotheses against the strongest baselines on the same scalar Fourier model. First, keeping the WGS weights but replacing the phase update by conjugate-gradient steps through the pixel-crosstalk kernel and the phase quantizer of the device (device-aware WGS) lowers the trap-intensity spread on the device. On a 10 x 10 lattice behind a crosstalk device, the relative standard deviation falls from a median of 5.21 percent for phase-fixed WGS at 30 iterations (5.21 percent at 100) to 0.205 percent, a median factor of 26 over 5 seeds (range 16 to 33) at a median 0.995 of the baseline's efficiency; the factor is 7.9 with 4-bit phase and a fill factor of 0.85 added, and 2.0 on a smaller 8 x 8 grid with flicker added and a fixed 30-iteration budget (the ratio of the means of 3 seeds); over the 5 geometries of the studio's benchmark on that device the median factor is 1.73 (0.97 to 4.69), and 2 of them meet both thresholds. A control that removes the device model from the loop gains nothing (5.14 percent), so the gain comes from the model. Second, optimizing every intermediate hologram of a moving-trap sequence with the trap phases locked to a smooth trajectory (flicker-bounded sequence) keeps the minimum transient intensity of the moving traps at a median 0.920 of their mean (range 0.915 to 0.932) over 5 seeds at 13 frames (below 0.9 at seven frames), against 0.654 (0.551 to 0.709) for linear phase interpolation. On longer moves, with the frames that keep the peak step per frame at most 0.2 Fourier units, the bound is met on 6 and 6 of 8 seeds of two lattice moves and on 5 of 6 seeds of a rearrangement case; the seeds that miss it miss it on the phase path their end phases prescribe, and at an equal number of frames on the rearrangement linear phase interpolation leads. Both results hold in a model of a simulated device and in a transient model that we define; neither is a hardware measurement. items.summary: A phase-only spatial light modulator in the pupil of a microscope objective can form hundreds to thousands of optical traps at once, but only if the phase pattern it displays is computed well: the pattern fixes how much light reaches the traps, how equal the traps are, where stray light goes, how the pattern survives a real device, and how fast it can be recomputed when traps move. DinHot is an open studio that runs 24 methods (19 published ones and 5 proposed here) on the same task, with the same seeds, metrics and device model, in Python as the reference and in a TypeScript port that runs live in a browser. We describe the optical and device model, the methods with the measured acceptance of each, 14 cases from a 3 x 3 array to a disordered 819-trap array and shaped potentials, the benchmark protocol, two learned models, and the 5 proposed methods, three of which meet their acceptance criteria on their acceptance tasks, each within a scope that the benchmark or the scope measurements narrow (a device-aware weighted Gerchberg-Saxton update, a flicker-bounded phase-continuous sequence and an efficiency-uniformity front), one of which meets a narrowed criterion (an aberration-robust hologram) and one of which is refuted by measurement (a learned warm start for phase-fixed weighted GS). A network trained on three-plane volumes beats its baseline at equal wall-clock on all 162 held-out volumes (median accuracy ratio 1.140), whereas its two-dimensional counterpart ties with Gerchberg-Saxton (ratio 0.9994). The model is a scalar Fourier model of a simulated device, not a calibrated instrument. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CEFOP_DinHot . items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents embedded in software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms inherit the user's permissions. When a permission is revoked during a task, the platform rejects the next read, but the agent still retains the data it previously retrieved in its context, drafts, saved documents, and memory. This study examined how platforms can enforce a mid-task revocation on that working state. The author defined correct behavior for four revocation types, each mapped to an obligation to block, purge, or suspend, including leaks through paraphrases, aggregates, and existence hints. The author built RevBench, a simulated field-service platform, and compared nine enforcement designs from access control, information-flow control, and machine unlearning on six frontier models in 6,048 runs. Outputs were scored using exact matching and two large-language-model judges. Per-call authorization still failed in 417 of 720 runs (57.9%), rising from 34.4% when the revocation preceded retrieval to 72.8% when it followed delivery. Information-flow labels leaked the least (12.9%) but left revoked data saved in 44.2% of runs. Designs that invalidated the context performed best, while editing the context in place left derived facts behind. A full restart and selective replay with listing-level provenance reached 21.4% and 21.0% substantive failure, the latter with 12.1% fewer model calls. Most remaining failures were disclosures about the restriction, often repeating the platform’s own notice, and larger models did not reduce them. SaaS platforms need revocation controls that reach the agent’s working state and match the type of revocation. items.summary: Overview Many continuous treatments are published only in classes, for example broadband connections per 1,000 households in the FCC Form 477 tract files. The paper studies difference-in-differences when the dose is observed only up to an interval. It characterizes what midpoint and two-way fixed effects regressions recover, derives sharp identified sets for the dose–response function under Lipschitz and monotonicity restrictions, and provides uniformly valid moment-inequality confidence sets. This package contains the code and derived data needed to reproduce the simulations, the empirical applications, and all tables and figures. Contents Identification and inference. Sharp identified sets via chain inequalities (Theorem 5.3, Corollary 5.4); sharp sets with overlapping intervals over admissible orderings (Proposition 5.7); GMS confidence sets with Gaussian and wild cluster bootstrap critical values (Sections 6.4, 6.8 and 7.6); decomposition of staggered TWFE regressions with interval doses (Proposition 4.6). Monte Carlo simulations. Factorial design with 1,000 replications per cell (Section 7, Tables 3–4); sharp versus outer confidence sets; calibration of the Lipschitz constant; few clusters; power; comparison with midpoint, dichotomized and bin-mean estimators (Supplementary Appendix A6–A7). Applications. County dose intervals built from FCC tract classes; household unbanked status from the FDIC National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households; bank branches by county from the FDIC Summary of Deposits; pre-period placebo tests and event studies; tract-level design exercise (Section 8, Supplementary Appendix A8). Figures. Illustration of identified sets (Figure 1) and event-study contrasts (Figure 3). Derived data included county_dose.csv : county dose intervals, December 2008 and December 2016, from FCC Form 477 tract classes (3,138 counties). sod_county_1999_2019.csv : bank branches and deposits by county and year, 1999–2019, aggregated from the FDIC Summary of Deposits. JSON files with the simulation and estimation results reported in the paper. Source data (not redistributed; public) FCC Form 477, residential fixed connections per 1,000 households by census tract: https://www.fcc.gov/general/broadband-deployment-data-fcc-form-477 FDIC National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households, public-use multi-year file: https://www.fdic.gov/household-survey FDIC Summary of Deposits, BankFind Suite API: https://api.fdic.gov/banks/sod (retrieved 30 October 2026) How to reproduce Requires Python 3 with numpy, pandas, scipy, matplotlib, xlrd and statsmodels (see requirements.txt ). The README maps each script to the tables and figures it produces and gives the order of execution. Random seeds are fixed in each script.

items.summary: The calibration and test probabilities of every run of a tabular classification benchmark, released so that prediction sets and their metrics can be recomputed without refitting a model. A conformal set is a function of four arrays: the class probabilities and labels on a calibration split, and the same on a test split. This deposit is those arrays, together with the software that reads them. The benchmark comprises 218 classification datasets and 22 models from four families, among them 13 tabular foundation models, each evaluated with the same ten seeds. Of the 218, 178 are real datasets and 40 are a synthetic block generated for this benchmark; three of the real ones are Bayesian-network resamplings of small classical datasets and are much larger than their seeds; of those, only one has its own seed in the collection, so that pair is not independent of itself while a rank test treats datasets as independent. Dataset size does not indicate provenance: the largest datasets in the collection are real. Coverage is not uniform and the per-model dataset count is reported for every cell. Eleven datasets carry more than ten classes, and the in-context models measured on them cannot enter them: one refuses and names the limit, another builds a ten-output head and fails inside a kernel. That is a capability limit observed on the models that were run rather than a property claimed of the family, and it is not missing work. One foundation model is measured on the original datasets only. Anything computed across models should be computed on a complete submatrix: the datasets on which every model being compared has all ten seeds. The calibration rows are held out of fitting, of tuning, of early stopping and of the in-context data, and each cell records which rows they were. The code that does it is included, with the line of each step documented. Probabilities are float64 and are not rounded: a prediction set is a comparison against a threshold, and a point sitting on that threshold moves if the value it is compared to is shortened. The data are released under CC BY 4.0. The software included in the source archive is released under the MIT licence, as stated by the LICENSE file it contains. The datasets themselves are not redistributed: each cell carries the row indices into its source dataset, and the synthetic datasets regenerate from their seeds with an included script. Model weights are not redistributed; every checkpoint is named in the model table. Version 1.2.0 adds the runs completed after version 1.1.0 and changes or removes nothing in it. Three new shards (cells-011 to cells-013, 2.02 GB) hold 311 further cells; index.parquet now lists all 46,182 cells and manifest_1016.parquet is their manifest. The files prefixed blocks_1016__ recompute the two blocks outside the main comparison on the completed runs, with the pipeline that produced the article's tables: the large-dataset block on 49 datasets and 21 models (42 in version 1.1.0) and the many-class block on 11 datasets and 7 models (5 in version 1.1.0). The main block of 113 real datasets and 22 models is unchanged. CHANGELOG.md lists what is added and the pairs that are still missing, with the reason for each.
items.title: TabSets: calibration and test probabilities for set-valued evaluation of tabular classifiers

items.summary: This Python software provides a Docker-based workflow for electroencephalography (EEG) quality control, preprocessing and feature extraction . It supports reproducible research on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children and adolescents using the task recordings in the BALLADEER dataset. The software documents and implements the processing workflow underlying A task EEG dataset with preprocessed signals and features for ADHD research in children and adolescents . That companion resource contains 669 eligible recordings from 156 participants and 115 feature definitions or templates across seven feature families. The recordings and generated feature tables are distributed separately from this software. What the software does Raw EEG quality assessment: characterizes recording quality before preprocessing and produces structured quality summaries. Recording eligibility and correction plans: applies the supplied, frozen label-blind selection records, including recording eligibility and approved channel-interpolation actions. Conservative EEG preprocessing: processes continuous blocks without bridging acquisition gaps, applies 0.5–40 Hz filtering, harmonizes sampling to 128 Hz, and performs conditional channel interpolation and average referencing. Post-preprocessing quality assessment: calculates quality summaries and comparisons with the original recordings. EEG feature extraction: generates seven feature families using aligned, gap-aware windows of 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds with 50% overlap, subject to each estimator's duration requirements. Output verification: checks processing lineage, cross-stage consistency and recorded checksums. The supplied selection records preserve the decisions used for the companion dataset. Reusing those records does not repeat the original manual review or establish new eligibility decisions for another cohort. Seven EEG feature families Temporal and statistical features. Conventional spectral features. Aperiodic spectral features. Complexity and fractal features. Functional connectivity features. Graph and network features. Time-frequency decomposition features. Feature definitions expand across channels, channel pairs and other indexed positions. Outputs retain calculation states and reasons for unavailable or undefined values. Duration-dependent support is explicit; for example, the configured aperiodic spectral analysis uses 8- and 16-second windows. Supported recordings, inputs and outputs The input is the original BALLADEER dataset, version 2 , obtained from its version-specific Figshare record . Extract the source data before running the software. The companion Zenodo derivative dataset is an output resource, not the input to this complete reproduction workflow. The packaged workflow is configured for five BALLADEER task conditions: CogniFit cognitive assessment, Attention Robots, and Slackline levels 1, 6 and 11. Users also provide a writable output directory. The input directory is mounted read-only. Outputs include preprocessed EEG signals in MNE-FIF format, tabular feature outputs, quality summaries, calculation-state records, configuration snapshots, processing manifests and checksums. The software archive includes label-blind selection metadata with pseudonymous recording identifiers; it does not contain the original EEG recordings or the generated derivative dataset. Reproducibility and package contents The archive includes Python source code, scientific configurations, a Dockerfile, version-pinned Python dependencies, shell launchers, validation tests and documentation. Users can run individual processing stages, extract one feature family for one task, or execute the complete sequential workflow. Graph features use the corresponding connectivity outputs. items.summary: This archive contains the replication package for the article "Are colour-coded economies empirically distinct? A cross-country test of economic specialisation" (submitted to Structural Change and Economic Dynamics). items.summary: Everything needed to redo the two analyses reported in the Technical Note named in the title, and nothing else. What is here the secondary analysis of published length-resolved binding: the contract frozen before any test statistic was computed and its two dated amendments, the resampling of the source's own trimmed-mean procedure, the anchored and anchor-free tests, the post-hoc robustness check across five normalisation variants, the superseded first run kept so the correction stays visible, and the figure generator; the two propositions behind the simulation and the script that checks both against the stored benchmark, per replicate; the simulated measurement study it checks: frozen primary and stress designs, the finite-chain engine, 7,200 simulated datasets under seven observation operators reported as all 302,400 planned rows including the undefined, outside-window and non-identified slots, an independent validator, the stress results, five focused tests, an 83-file manifest and a dependency lock; an 80-value subset of the Source Data for Fig. 2B/C of Sheikh et al., Nat. Commun. 13, 3617 (2022), with its sheet coordinates. These values keep the original article's CC BY 4.0 licence and attribution; the rest of the archive is under the MIT licence in LICENSE. Reproducing The added analysis runs from the archive root with the standard library plus NumPy; the README gives the four commands. It was re-run on an interpreter far older than the one that produced the shipped results (Python 3.7.6 with NumPy 1.19.1, against 3.13.17 with 2.5.3): the proposition checks were identical in all 520 compared values apart from the recorded environment, and three bootstrap interval endpoints differed in their last digits, by at most 1.5e-11. Figures redraw with the same layout; their byte sequences depend on which sans-serif face the host has. The base study's own replay script requires bit equality and returns a failure on Linux, where ten of its twenty tables differ in their last digits. What is deliberately not here the manuscript text; the original publisher workbook of Sheikh et al. and every panel of it other than the 80 values used; historical MCMC traces and the exploratory transcript analysis of an earlier, separate study, which this work does not use; correspondence and author-only files. REDACTION.md lists the three files whose description of the work was restated for publication, with the digest before and after; no number, method, decision rule or result changed. Scope Synthetic counts are idealised events, not biological replicates. The site-equivalent pool is not an alpha-dystroglycan molecule count, glycan mass, antibody intensity or muscle force. The published array values are technical replicates of one experiment, and the source states no independent experiments. No real assay's detection ceiling or recovery function is measured anywhere in this archive.

items.summary: Genetic mutations can lead to disease by disrupting molecular interactions, altering protein stability, inducing misfolding, and promoting protein aggregation. Although existing predictive models have achieved promising performance, they often lack mechanistic interpretability and fail to fully incorporate the underlying physical and chemical principles governing mutation-induced effects. Moreover, current approaches typically address disease association, protein stability changes, and solubility alterations as separate prediction tasks rather than integrating them within a unified framework. In this study, we introduce a multiscale commutative algebra modeling framework for predicting disease-mutation association. Leveraging persistent Stanley-Reisner theory, we extract algebraic invariants to build two predictive models: Commutative Algebra Neural Network (CANet) and Commutative Algebra Gradient Boosting Tree (CATree). The proposed framework is applied to three biologically connected tasks: disease-associated mutation identification, mutation-induced protein stability change prediction, and mutation-induced protein solubility change classification. Across six benchmark tasks, CANet and CATree consistently achieve leading predictive performance, with up to 7.5% relative improvement over existing methods. These results demonstrate that commutative algebra provides a unified, interpretable, and generalizable modeling strategy for mutation-disease association prediction.
items.title: Commutative Algebra Modeling of Mutation and Disease Association

items.summary: Abstract: Classical inferential statistics and p-value hypothesis testing in healthcare big data repositories suffer from severe structural limitations, notably p-hacking, asymptotic N-bias, and the frequent violation of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumptions due to intra-patient longitudinal dependencies, hospital clustering, and epidemiological shockwaves. To overcome these failures, we introduce an Inverse Breakpoint Analysis, a scale-invariant, physics-inspired metrological audit framework. Our analysis treats discrete clinical event counts not as abstract probabilities, but as physical informational mass. Grounded in Garwood exact discrete limits and Wilson-Hilferty approximations, the framework extends our previous work on stress testing indices for Big health data and establishes three rigorous thresholds: a pure mass saturation limit, a baseline tolerance band, and a structural signal threshold. Through the use of these three parameters, our inverse break-point analysis eliminates false-positive artifacts induced by massive repository sizes while preventing under-powering in small cohorts. Ultimately, the framework demonstrates that percentage-based thresholds are kinematic artifacts of scale, whereas absolute excess discrete mass serves as the sole physical invariant for healthcare data validation. We validated this approach with numerous illustrative examples.
items.title: Inverse Breakpoint Analysis: A Scale-Invariant Physics-Inspired Metrological Audit for Sanitary Big Data

items.summary: APEP — JGR manuscript release ( paper-jgr-v1.0 ) Code, data products and figures supporting the manuscript on the ionospheric response to the 14 October 2023 annular and 8 April 2024 total Great American Eclipses (GAEs). Summary We present a multipoint investigation of the ionospheric response to the 14 October 2023 annular and 8 April 2024 total Great American Eclipses (GAEs) using coordinated observations from five Digisondes, the Wallops Island VIPIR, the Millstone Hill incoherent scatter radar, and continental-scale GNSS TEC measurements. Key results Clear E- and F2-region depletions in both events across peak obscurations of 0.30–0.82, observed at local times 10:24–15:22 LT. E region depletion scales quasi-linearly with obscuration; the F2 region lags peak obscuration by 20–30 min, consistent with the longer O⁺ recombination timescale. No G-condition (NmF1 ≥ NmF2) in either event, even at 0.82 obscuration: high obscuration alone is insufficient without adequate F2-peak height reduction and favourable local-time/seasonal conditions. White Sands skymaps show a bifurcated echo population during the 2024 recovery phase; Wallops VIPIR frequency–time–intensity plots show cusp-like features confined to 3–6 MHz. Idealized ray tracing shows both signatures can arise from eclipse-excited wave structures at different horizontal scales, i.e. distinct HF manifestations of a common wave field. GNSS TEC : along-track relative change in minima exceeds 40 % (2023 and 2024) relative to the expected baseline. Figures in this release All manuscript figures are in manuscript_figures/jgr/ (PNG, plus PDF where produced). Generating code is in apep/jgr/ . Figures 2 and 4 (ionosonde time series) were redone as 5×4 grids: rows are the five stations sorted by peak obscuration; columns are foF2, h′F2/hmF2, foE, h′E/hmE. Each panel shows the eclipse-day series (smoothed, gaps ≤ 90 min interpolated) against the quiet-day median, with the eclipse interval shaded and the peak obscuration 𝒪ᵖ₁₉₃ annotated. Journal-style fonts, thin lines, no heavy markers; AGU double-column width. Figure 2 (2023, 13–21 UT) is built entirely from Datasets/Data/*_scaled.csv and *_median.csv ; WS833/KR835 use the despiked event files in Datasets/processing/final/ when present. Figure 4 (2024, 16–21 UT) is built from SAO data via jgr_2024_scaled.py . Shared code: apep/jgr/jgr_timeseries_5x4.py ( jgr_2023_scaled.py is a thin wrapper). Known data caveats AU930 h′E sits in 100–110 km steps against an ~85 km median (2023); the 2024 AU930 hmE median CSV is flat at 110 km. AU930 foF2 saturates near 9.9 MHz after ~18:30 UT (2023). BC840 h′F2 shows a ~340 km excursion near maximum obscuration (2023). KR835/WS833 median CSVs lack true hmF2/hmE; 2024 KR835/WS833 median CSVs do not exist (baseline falls back to the SAO mean); WS833 2024 has no data. Reproducing the time-series figures conda run -n apep python -m apep.jgr.jgr_timeseries_5x4 --year 2023 # Figure 2 conda run -n apep python apep/jgr/jgr_2024_scaled.py # Figure 4
